2004-Q15a.q: In your drawing of a synapse, what must separate the two neurons?

2025-Q14c.board: What is the function of a Schwann cell?
2025-Q14c.hook: Schwann cells roll round the axon like a Swiss roll, making its coat

2025-Q14c.q: Give one possible cause and one treatment of Parkinson's disease or paralysis, saying which. (2 points)
wrong: Parkinson's: too much dopamine; treated with antibiotics
Paralysis: inherited lack of dopamine; treated with insulin
Parkinson's: lack of insulin; treated with antibiotics
2025-Q14c.why: A matching cause and treatment: Parkinson's from low dopamine or genes, treated with L-dopa or physiotherapy; paralysis from spinal cord damage, physio.
2025-Q14c.hint: Choose one disorder. Then: what goes wrong in the brain or cord, and what helps?
2025-Q14c.hook: Parkinson's can run in families: genes plus low dopamine

2026-Q7e.q: Give the precise location and the main function of the cerebellum. (2 points)
2026-Q7e.right: At the back of the brain; it coordinates movement and balance
wrong: At the front of the brain; it controls memory and thought
At the back of the brain; it controls memory and thought
In the brain stem; it controls breathing and heartbeat
2026-Q7e.why: The cerebellum is at the back of the brain, under the cerebrum; it coordinates muscle movement, balance and posture.
2026-Q7e.hint: It's the 'little brain' tucked under the big one. What goes wrong if it's damaged?
2026-Q7e.hook: The cerebellum at the back keeps you balanced: think of a tightrope walker

2026-Q17d.q: Name the fluid found in the central canal of the spinal cord.
wrong: Lymph
Tissue fluid
Plasma
2026-Q17d.why: The central canal and the spaces round the brain hold cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which cushions and nourishes the CNS.
2026-Q17d.hint: Its name joins the two parts of the CNS: the brain (cerebrum) and the spinal cord.
2026-Q17d.hook: Cerebro (brain) + spinal (cord): the CNS's own cushioning fluid

2026-Q17d.q: Name tissue Y, with three layers, and one other structure that protects the spinal cord. (2 points)
wrong: The myelin sheath, and the vertebrae (backbone)
The meninges, and the skull
The white matter, and the ribs
2026-Q17d.why: Y is the meninges, three membranes round the CNS; the spinal cord is also protected by the vertebrae (and cerebrospinal fluid).
2026-Q17d.hint: Three thin layers wrap it, and a column of bones surrounds those. Name both.
2026-Q17d.board: Name the three-layered tissue around the spinal cord, and one other structure that protects it. (2 points)
2026-Q17d.hook: Spinal cord armour: three meninges inside a column of vertebrae

2026-Q17d.q: P is the pale outer region and Q the darker core. Name them. (2 points)
2026-Q17d.right: Outer: white matter; core: grey matter
wrong: Outer: grey matter; core: white matter
Outer: meninges; core: white matter
Outer: myelin sheath; core: central canal
2026-Q17d.why: In the spinal cord, white matter (myelinated axons) is outside and grey matter (cell bodies) forms the core; in the brain it is the other way round.
2026-Q17d.hint: Myelin is pale. In the spinal cord, are the myelinated fibres inside or outside?
2026-Q17d.board: In a cross section of the spinal cord, name the pale outer region and the darker core. (2 points)
2026-Q17d.hook: The spinal cord: a grey butterfly wrapped in white

2026-Q17d.q: What three parts must your drawing of a neuron show?
2026-Q17d.right: Dendrites, a cell body with a nucleus, and an axon
wrong: Dendrites, a cell wall and an axon
A nucleus, a vacuole and an axon
A cell body, a synaptic cleft and a cell wall
2026-Q17d.why: The drawing needs dendrites, a cell body with its nucleus, and an axon: miss one and you lose half the marks, miss two and you get none.
2026-Q17d.hint: Think of a tree: the branches, the trunk's base with its nucleus, and one long root.
2026-Q17d.board: What three main parts make up a neuron?
2026-Q17d.hook: Branches, body, long tail: dendrites, cell body, axon

2026-Q17d.q: On your neuron, which part do you label as a dendrite?
2026-Q17d.right: A short branch on the cell body
wrong: The long fibre leaving the cell body
The fatty layer around the axon
The gap at the end of the axon
2026-Q17d.why: Dendrites are the short branches on the cell body; the axon is the long fibre, and the myelin sheath the fatty layer round it.
2026-Q17d.hint: Three labels: the branches, the long fibre and its coat. Which are the branches?
2026-Q17d.board: Which part of a neuron is a dendrite?
2026-Q17d.hook: Dendrites = little twigs on the cell body
keys: short branches on the cell body

2026-Q17d.q: On your diagram, which way should the impulse arrow point?
2026-Q17d.right: From the dendrites towards the axon
wrong: From the axon towards the dendrites
Into the cell body from the axon
Both ways along the axon
2026-Q17d.why: The impulse travels from the dendrites, through the cell body and away along the axon: point the arrow away from the cell body.
2026-Q17d.hint: Where does a neuron pick up messages, and where does it pass them on?
2026-Q17d.board: In which direction does an impulse travel through a neuron?
2026-Q17d.hook: D, C, A: Dendrites, Cell body, Axon, always that way

2026-Q17d.q: Describe the mechanism of a reflex action. (3 points)
2026-Q17d.right: Impulse goes along sensory neuron, then interneuron, then motor neuron
wrong: Impulse goes along motor neuron, then interneuron, then sensory neuron
Impulse goes along sensory neuron straight to the brain, which decides
A hormone travels in the blood from the receptor to the muscle
2026-Q17d.why: Three of: a receptor detects the stimulus, the impulse travels along a sensory neuron, through an interneuron in the CNS, along a motor neuron, to the effector.
2026-Q17d.hint: Name the three neurons the impulse passes through, in order. And say 'impulse'!
2026-Q17d.hook: Receptor, sensory, inter, motor, effector: say 'impulse' or lose a mark

S1-Q1b.q: Identify molecule A and structure B, the sac holding it. (2 points)
S1-Q1b.right: Neurotransmitter, stored in a synaptic vesicle
wrong: Hormone, stored in a synaptic vesicle
Neurotransmitter, stored in a Schwann cell
Enzyme, stored in the synaptic cleft
S1-Q1b.why: A is a neurotransmitter, e.g. acetylcholine; B is a synaptic vesicle, a sac that stores it until an impulse arrives.
S1-Q1b.hint: A crosses the gap to carry the message; B is the little bubble it waits in.
S1-Q1b.board: At a synapse, name the chemical that crosses the gap and the sac that stores it. (2 points)
S1-Q1b.hook: Vesicles are water balloons full of neurotransmitter, popped by the impulse

S1-Q1b.q: Which way is a nerve impulse passed across a synapse?
S1-Q1b.right: From the neuron with vesicles to the one with receptors
wrong: From the neuron with receptors to the one with vesicles
Both ways across the cleft
Along the cleft, parallel to the membranes
S1-Q1b.why: Vesicles are only in the presynaptic neuron and receptors only on the postsynaptic one, so the impulse crosses one way only.
S1-Q1b.hint: Which side releases the chemical, and which side has the receptors that catch it?
S1-Q1b.hook: One-way traffic: vesicles send, receptors receive

S1-Q1b.q: What happens to molecules A after the nerve impulse transmission is complete? (2 points)
S1-Q1b.right: Broken down by an enzyme; the products are reabsorbed and reused
wrong: Carried away in the blood to the kidneys
They stay bound to the receptors for good
Made into myelin by the Schwann cells
S1-Q1b.why: An enzyme in the cleft (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) breaks the transmitter down, and the presynaptic neuron reabsorbs the products to make more.
S1-Q1b.hint: If it stayed, the next neuron would fire non-stop. What clears it, and is any of it reused?
S1-Q1b.board: What happens to a neurotransmitter after it has passed on an impulse? (2 points)
S1-Q1b.hook: Clean up and recycle: an enzyme breaks it down, the knob takes the bits back
